newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees no early end to British beef ban.
newsitem.headline: EU sees no early end to British beef ban.

text.p: European Union farm ministers gave a cautious welcome on Tuesday to Britain's decision to slaughter 100,000 extra cattle, but warned it could be a long haul before a worldwide ban on British beef exports was lifted.
"The announcement is welcome," Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler was quoted as telling ministers at a farm Council. "But further steps need to be taken. We have no British proposal yet."
Fischler was speaking after British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg briefed ministers on a statement he made to the British parliament on Monday.
The cull was first agreed at an EU summit in Florence in June as part of a deal to end the mad cow crisis and restore consumer confidence in beef.
But Britain shelved it in September after new scientific evidence came to light that the disease, properly known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) would die out naturally in five years.
The EU banned British beef exports in March after London disclosed that BSE, which has ravaged British herds, could be caught by people who ate infected beef.

Hogg told ministers he would present proposals to the EU early in 1997 to exempt herds which have not been fed contaminated meat and bone meal, which is blamed for the outbreak, and which have been tracked since birth.

Northern Irish herds are expected to be the first to benefit from this initial step towards ending the global ban as they have been fed on grass, and have been registered on a computer database for the past six years.
Britain's U-turn in its cull policy came after the government lost its parliamentary majority and was forced to rely on the support of Ulster Unionists, officials noted.

Hogg said Britain was able to implement the selective cull because it had cleared a backlog in a much larger, separate scheme to slaughter older animals which had removed more than one million animals from the food chain.
Britain has now concluded that the scientific evidence on the time it would take for BSE to die out was unlikely to change decisively the need for the cull, he added.
Fischler said Britain's delay in complying with the Florence agreement could have undermined consumer confidence.
Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates said the British move was a step forward and he was impatient to receive the British proposals which would be studied by EU scientific committees.
"1996 was a very traumatic year for the British beef industry. I hope 1997 will be better," an Irish spokesman quoted him as saying.
Officials said that no other ministers spoke during the brief discussion.
But Dutch farm minister Jozias Van Aartsen said on Monday that the ban would only be lifted in stages and talks would continue through the Dutch EU presidency in the first six months of next year.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert, whose country was the toughest in protecting public health, was also cautious.
"For the moment, I don't see any possibility for a regional relaxation or for certain products," he told Reuters on Monday. "It will take time."
Portugal was sceptical, criticising Britain for wasting six months in implementing the Florence agreement, and calling the British statement was too vague.
"There's still nothing on the table," an aide to Portuguese Farm Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva said.
Hogg agreed a long battle lay ahead. "I would not say it will take years but we have got quite a long way to travel," he said in a British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) television interview.
